Regicide is a noun with two closely related meanings:

  1. The act of killing a king, queen, or any reigning monarch.
  2. A person who kills a king, queen, or any reigning monarch.

Both meanings revolve around the same event — the killing of a monarch — but one names the act itself, and the other names the person who did it.

Think of it this way: there are specific words in English for killing specific kinds of people.

  • Killing a human being = homicide
  • Killing a fellow citizen = fratricide (loosely used)
  • Killing one's own father = patricide
  • Killing a king or queen = regicide

What makes regicide special as a word — and as a concept — is the identity of the victim. The victim must be a reigning monarch: a king, queen, emperor, or empress who is currently sitting on the throne and ruling a nation. This is the detail that matters most. It is not about how they were killed — whether by sword, poison, gunshot, or public execution — it is about who was killed.
The Two Noun Senses in Use

Sense 1 — The act:

"The regicide of the king sent shockwaves across all of Europe."

Here, "regicide" means the killing itself — the event of a monarch being killed.

Sense 2 — The person:

"The regicides were hunted down and punished for what they had done."

Here, "regicides" (plural) refers to the people who carried out the killing of a monarch. One person who kills a king = one regicide. A group of people who collectively kill or cause the death of a king = multiple regicides.

Both uses are correct and common. Context will almost always make it clear which sense is meant.
Who Counts as a Victim of Regicide?

The victim must be a reigning (currently ruling) monarch. This distinction matters:

  • A sitting king or queen who is killed → regicide. ✅
  • A king who already abdicated (gave up the throne) and is later killed → traditionally, this is debated, though many still call it regicide in common usage.
  • A prince who has not yet become king and is killed → not regicide in the strict sense.
  • A president or prime minister who is killed → not regicide, because they are not monarchs. (Killing a head of state who is not a monarch has its own term: tyrannicide, if the ruler was considered a tyrant, though this is a less common word.)

The core idea is: a monarch who holds the crown at the time of death.
Why Was Regicide Treated as Such a Serious Crime Historically?

This word carries enormous historical and cultural weight, and understanding why helps you grasp how powerful the concept is.

For most of human history, kings and queens were not seen simply as powerful politicians. They were believed to rule by what was called "divine right" — the idea that God had personally chosen them to rule, and that their authority came directly from heaven. The king was not just a person; he was the living symbol of the entire nation, its laws, its God-given order, and its people.

This meant that killing a king was not just murder. It was considered:

  • An act of treason — a betrayal of the highest order against one's own country.
  • An act of sacrilege — an offense against God, since the king was seen as God's representative on earth.
  • An act of chaos — it threatened to collapse the entire political and social structure of a nation, since everything revolved around the monarch.

Because of all this, regicide was historically treated as one of the gravest possible crimes, often worse in the eyes of the law and society than any ordinary murder. Those convicted of regicide (or of planning it) typically faced the most severe punishments possible — public execution, torture, or the execution of their entire family.

Understanding the word through real events makes it stick.

1. King Charles I of England (1649)
King Charles I was put on trial by the English Parliament during the English Civil War. He was found guilty of treason against his own people and was publicly beheaded. The men who signed his death warrant were called regicides. Even decades later, after the monarchy was restored, those regicides who were still alive were hunted down and severely punished.

2. King Louis XVI of France (1793)
During the French Revolution, King Louis XVI was tried and guillotined by the revolutionary government. This event is one of the most discussed regicides in world history. Those who voted for his execution were also referred to as regicides.

3. Tsar Nicholas II of Russia (1918)
The last emperor of Russia, Nicholas II, along with his entire family, was shot and killed by Bolshevik revolutionaries. This is widely regarded as one of the most tragic acts of regicide in modern history.

4. Julius Caesar (44 BC)
Though Caesar was not technically a king (he was a Roman dictator), his assassination by members of the Roman Senate is often informally discussed using the concept of regicide, since he held absolute power. The debate over whether his killing was regicide or tyrannicide is a genuinely interesting historical discussion.
Regicide as a Concept in Literature and Thought

Regicide has fascinated writers, philosophers, and political thinkers for centuries, precisely because it raises hard questions:

  • Can killing a ruler ever be justified?
  • Is a tyrant's life worth protecting just because they wear a crown?
  • Who has the right to decide that a monarch should die?

Shakespeare's play Macbeth is perhaps the most famous literary exploration of regicide. Macbeth kills the rightful King Duncan to take the throne for himself, and the entire play examines the psychological, moral, and political consequences of that act — the guilt, the unraveling of a person's mind, and the chaos it unleashes.

In political philosophy, thinkers have debated whether tyrannicide (killing a tyrant) is ever morally acceptable, and whether a monarch who becomes a tyrant still deserves the protection that the word "regicide" implies.

• Regicide does not imply a judgment about whether the killing was right or wrong. It is a neutral descriptive word. The execution of a cruel tyrant-king and the assassination of a beloved peaceful queen are both regicide — the word does not take sides.
  • The word can be used in historical, legal, literary, and journalistic contexts. It is not an everyday casual word; it carries weight and seriousness whenever it is used.
  • Occasionally, in figurative or metaphorical language, writers use "regicide" to describe the symbolic or political destruction of a monarch's power — not a literal killing but the complete removal of a ruler's authority. This is rare and always clearly metaphorical in context.

What it namesThe killing of a reigning monarch, OR the person who kills a reigning monarch
VictimA king, queen, emperor, or empress who is currently ruling
Historical weightConsidered among the gravest crimes in history — treason, sacrilege, and chaos combined
ToneSerious, weighty, formal — not casual language
Famous examplesCharles I (England), Louis XVI (France), Nicholas II (Russia)

Regicide is ultimately a word about power, legitimacy, and the ultimate transgression — the killing of the person who represents the entire authority of a state. That is why it has its own dedicated word, its own moral gravity, and its own permanent place in history, law, and literature.
